 Remember every listed NAS here is diskless, budget drives separately
 The price shown for a NAS enclosure covers the hardware chassis, CPU, and RAM only, not the actual storage drives, NAS-grade drives built for 24/7 operation like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red still need to be budgeted on top, often adding $80 to $200 or more per bay depending on capacity and drive type.
 This matters because comparing NAS units purely by enclosure price without factoring in drive cost gives a misleading picture of the real total investment, a cheaper enclosure with more bays to fill can end up costing more overall than a pricier enclosure with fewer bays.
 Check whether a listing is diskless or ships with drives included, and add realistic per-bay drive costs to the enclosure price before comparing total cost across options.
 Weigh CPU class and RAM over bay count for real day-to-day performance
 Bay count determines maximum storage capacity, but CPU architecture (Intel, AMD, or ARM) and RAM amount determine how well the NAS actually handles real workloads, running apps, transcoding media on the fly, or serving multiple simultaneous users, and a higher bay count with a weak CPU can bottleneck performance regardless of how much raw storage it holds.
 This matters more the more the NAS will do beyond simple file storage, like Plex transcoding or running multiple docker containers, less if it's purely a basic backup target.
 Check the specific CPU model and RAM amount (and whether RAM is upgradeable) rather than choosing primarily by bay count.
 Understand RAID as a rebuild-time safety net, not a substitute for real backup
 RAID configurations protect against a single drive failure by letting the array rebuild from redundant data, but RAID is not a backup, it does nothing to protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a controller failure that affects the whole array at once.
 This distinction matters because treating RAID redundancy as sufficient backup protection is a common and genuinely risky misunderstanding, a real backup strategy needs a copy of critical data stored somewhere physically separate from the NAS itself.
 Check what RAID level a given NAS supports, and separately plan an actual backup strategy, ideally following a 3-2-1 approach, rather than relying on RAID redundancy alone.
 Match drive type (HDD vs SSD/NVMe) to your actual access pattern
 Traditional hard drives offer the lowest cost per terabyte for bulk storage like media libraries or backups, while SSD or NVMe-based NAS storage costs significantly more per terabyte but delivers much faster random access speeds, genuinely useful for frequently-accessed files, active project work, or serving as a fast cache tier.

 Check whether the NAS supports the drive type you need, and weigh the real cost-per-terabyte difference against how much you'll actually benefit from faster random access.
 Consider noise level if the NAS will run continuously in a shared living or office space
 A NAS that runs 24/7 generates continuous fan and drive noise, and that noise profile varies meaningfully between models, some use larger, slower-spinning fans that stay genuinely quiet, while others rely on smaller, faster fans that produce a persistent whine noticeable in a quiet room.
 This matters a great deal if the NAS will sit in a bedroom, living room, or shared home office rather than a dedicated closet or basement out of earshot.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Will my Time Machine backups stop working because AFP is being removed?
 If your NAS is still configured to use AFP, yes, backups will silently stop once your Mac updates past macOS 27. Every NAS in this list supports SMB3 with Bonjour/mDNS advertising, which is the protocol combination Apple is standardizing on, but confirm SMB3 is actually enabled in your sharing settings rather than assuming it by default.
 Why does my Time Machine backup keep growing and filling up the NAS?
 Time Machine stores backups in a sparse bundle disk image that expands automatically over time, and without a manually set quota it will keep growing until it consumes all available NAS space. Set a quota in the NAS admin panel during initial setup, a common recommendation is roughly 1.5x your Mac's internal storage capacity.
 Can multiple Macs back up to the same NAS with Time Machine?
 Yes, but each Mac needs its own separate shared folder with its own quota. Using a single shared folder for more than one Mac's Time Machine backup will corrupt the backup history for both machines, so set up a dedicated folder per Mac even within the same household.
 How long does the first Time Machine backup take over a NAS?
 For a 512GB Mac, an initial full Time Machine backup over Wi-Fi can take 8-24 hours depending on your router, and considerably less over a wired Ethernet connection. Run the first backup wired if at all possible; incremental backups afterward are small enough to run comfortably over Wi-Fi.
 How do I know my Time Machine backup will actually restore if I need it?
 A backup can appear to complete successfully for months while quietly failing to produce a restorable image due to RAID errors or file corruption. Periodically, at least once a quarter, test an actual file or folder restore from the backup rather than relying on Time Machine's success indicator alone.
 Do drive compatibility warnings mean I bought the wrong drive?
 Not necessarily. Some 2024-and-newer Plus-tier NAS models show a compatibility warning in the admin panel for any drive that isn't the manufacturer's own branded line, even when a reputable third-party NAS drive like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red works fine. It's worth knowing before you buy so the warning doesn't seem like a hardware failure.

 Backup disks you can use with Time Machine - Apple Support 
 Backup disks you can use with Time Machine
 Time Machine can back up your Mac to any of these storage devices.
 External storage device connected to Mac 
 Mac shared as a network backup destination 
 Network-attached storage (NAS) device 
 AirPort Extreme Base Station or AirPort Time Capsule 
 External storage device connected to Mac
 Time Machine can back up to an external storage device connected to a compatible port on your Mac , such as a USB-C or Thunderbolt port. This is the most common Time Machine setup.
 Compatibility : Some older versions of macOS created backup disks using Mac OS Extended as the file system format instead of APFS. If you have an existing Time Machine backup disk, and you chose to encrypt that backup, learn about support for encrypted Mac OS Extended disks in macOS 28 or later .
 Mac shared as a network backup destination
 Time Machine can back up to the built-in disk of another Mac on your network, or to an external storage device connected to that Mac. 
 Compatibility : This solution is recommended only when both computers are using macOS 11 or later . When either Mac is using an earlier macOS, network backup uses Apple Filing Protocol (AFP), which isn't supported in macOS 27 or later.
 macOS Ventura 13 or later
 On the Mac to be used as a Time Machine backup destination, choose System Settings from the Apple menu .
 Click General in the sidebar, then click Sharing on the right.
 Turn on File Sharing. If prompted, enter your administrator password.
 Click the More info button next to File Sharing.
 Click the Add button under the Shared Folders list, then choose a folder or external storage device to use for Time Machine backups.
 Control-click the folder or storage device that you added, then choose Advanced Options from the menu that appears.
 Select “Share as a Time Machine backup destination,” then click OK.
 When setting up Time Machine on other Mac computers that are connected to the same network, you can now select the shared folder or storage device as the backup disk.
 macOS Monterey 12 or macOS Big Sur 11
 On the Mac to be used as a Time Machine backup destination, choose System Preferences from the Apple menu .
 Click Sharing.
 From the list of services on the left, select File Sharing.
 Click the add button (+) under the Shared Folders list on the right, then choose a folder or external storage device to use for Time Machine backups.
 Control-click the folder that you added, then choose Advanced Options from the menu that appears.
 Select “Share as a Time Machine backup destination,” then click OK.
 When setting up Time Machine on other Mac computers that are connected to the same network, you can now select the shared folder or storage device as the backup disk.
 Network-attached storage (NAS) device
 Time Machine can back up to a third-party NAS device that supports Time Machine over the SMB network protocol. Check the documentation of your NAS device for help setting it up for use with Time Machine.
 Compatibility : Time Machine backup or other data transfer to or from NAS devices over Apple Filing Protocol (AFP) is not recommended and isn't supported in macOS 27 or later.
 AirPort Extreme Base Station or Time Capsule
 Compatibility : These solutions are no longer recommended, because Time Machine backup and other data transfer to or from these devices use Apple Filing Protocol (AFP), which isn't supported in macOS 27 or later.
 Time Machine can back up to the built-in disk of an AirPort Time Capsule on your network. Simply select the Time Capsule as the backup disk when setting up Time Machine on your Mac.
 Time Machine can also back up to an external storage device connected to the USB port of an AirPort Extreme Base Station (802.11ac model) or AirPort Time Capsule on your network:
 If the storage device isn’t using Mac OS Extended (Journaled) format, connect it to your Mac and reformat it with Disk Utility .
 Connect the storage device to a USB port on your base station, then turn it on.
 Open AirPort Utility, which is in the Utilities folder of your Applications folder. 
 Select your base station, then click Edit to view its settings.
 Click the Disks tab in the settings window.
 Select your backup disk from the list of partitions, then select “Enable file sharing”: 
 If more than one user on your network will back up to this disk with Time Machine, you can use the Secure Shared Disks pop-up menu to make sure that they can view only their own backups, not yours. Choose “With accounts” from the menu, then click the add button (+) to add users.
 Click Update to restart your base station and apply the settings.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Time Machine Backups?
 2-Bay vs 4-Bay: Which Do You Actually Need?
 For most households with 1-3 Macs, a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 (mirroring) provides the right balance of capacity and redundancy. RAID 1 writes the same data to both drives simultaneously, so if one drive fails, your entire Time Machine history survives on the other. A 2-bay unit with two 8TB drives gives you 8TB of usable mirrored storage, which holds roughly 5-7 years of Time Machine history for a typical household.
 4-bay NAS units make sense if you need more than 16TB of usable storage, run a creative business with large media files, or want RAID 5/6 configurations for better storage efficiency. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus and Synology DS425+ are my top picks in this category.
 SMB3 Verification: Why It Matters for Time Machine
 Apple deprecated AFP years ago, and modern macOS Time Machine requires SMB3 to function reliably. Before buying any NAS, verify it explicitly supports SMB3 protocol. All eight units in this guide passed my SMB3 verification test, which involved creating a Time Machine share and confirming macOS recognized it as a backup destination without manual protocol configuration.
 If your NAS only supports older SMB1/SMB2 protocols, you’ll experience failed backups, corruption errors, or the NAS simply not appearing in Time Machine’s destination list. This is the single most common reason a NAS “doesn’t work with Mac.” Every Synology and UGREEN unit in this roundup supports SMB3 natively.
 RAID Configuration Recommendations for Time Machine
 Always use RAID 1 (mirroring) at minimum for Time Machine storage pools. RAID 0 (striping) gives you more capacity but no redundancy – if one drive fails, you lose your entire backup history. RAID 5 and RAID 6 add parity for better capacity efficiency on 4-bay units, but require more advanced configuration.
 For most home users, two 8TB drives in RAID 1 provide enough capacity and bulletproof redundancy. Buy drives from the same batch when possible to minimize simultaneous failure risk, and replace drives proactively after 4-5 years of continuous use.
 Capacity Planning: How Much Storage Do You Need?
 Time Machine keeps hourly backups for 24 hours, daily backups for a month, and weekly backups until the disk fills up. A good rule of thumb is 2-3x the size of your Mac’s internal storage. If your MacBook has a 512GB SSD, plan for at least 1TB of NAS storage. If you have a 1TB MacBook, plan for 2-3TB.
 Multi-Mac households should add up the storage needs across all Macs and multiply by 2 for safe capacity. Set per-user quotas in your NAS settings to prevent one Mac’s backup from filling the entire pool.
 Setting Up Time Machine on Your NAS
 Step 1: Create a dedicated shared folder on your NAS for Time Machine backups. Step 2: Enable SMB3 protocol on the folder and set appropriate user permissions. Step 3: On your Mac, open System Settings > General > Time Machine, click “Add Backup Disk,” and select your NAS share from the list. Step 4: For initial backups, connect your Mac to the NAS via Ethernet – WiFi initial backups can take 3-7 days for a 512GB MacBook.
 Set user quotas in your NAS interface (DSM for Synology, UGOS for UGREEN) to prevent backups from consuming all available space. I recommend setting each Mac’s quota to 1.5-2x its internal storage size.
 Multi-Mac Backup Management
 Most modern NAS units handle multiple simultaneous Time Machine backups without issue. The Synology DS225+ and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus both managed 3 concurrent Mac backups in my testing without slowdown. Create separate shared folders for each Mac, or use a single folder with subfolders per Mac, depending on your NAS interface.
 Set distinct user accounts for each family member and assign per-user quotas. This prevents one Mac’s runaway backups from filling the entire pool and breaking everyone else’s backups.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I use a NAS for Time Machine backups?
 Yes, any NAS with SMB3 protocol support works as a Time Machine destination. Modern macOS requires SMB3 after Apple deprecated AFP. All NAS units in this guide support SMB3 natively and have been verified to work with Time Machine. Setup involves creating a shared folder on the NAS, enabling SMB, and selecting the NAS as a backup disk in macOS Time Machine settings.
 What is the best NAS for Time Machine backups?
 The Synology DS225+ is the best NAS for Time Machine backups for most users in 2026. It combines native SMB3 support, a polished DSM interface that makes Time Machine setup nearly automatic, and reliable multi-Mac support. Budget shoppers should consider the Synology DS223j, while power users with large storage needs should look at the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus.
 How do I set up Time Machine on a NAS?
 Step 1: Create a dedicated shared folder on your NAS for Time Machine. Step 2: Enable SMB3 protocol on the folder and set user permissions. Step 3: On your Mac, open System Settings u0026gt; General u0026gt; Time Machine, click Add Backup Disk, and select your NAS share. Step 4: Connect via Ethernet for initial backups – WiFi initial backups can take 3-7 days for a typical MacBook.
 What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
 The 3-2-1 backup rule means keeping 3 copies of your data on 2 different media types with 1 copy offsite. For Mac users, this typically means: one copy on your Mac, one copy on your NAS, and one copy in cloud storage (Backblaze, iCloud, or similar). This protects against drive failure, NAS failure, theft, fire, and ransomware. Most NAS units in this guide include built-in cloud backup integration.
 How much storage do I need for Time Machine?

Multi-Mac households should add storage needs across all Macs and multiply by 2. Set per-user quotas in your NAS settings to prevent one Mac from filling the entire pool.
 Final Verdict: Which Best NAS for Time Machine Backups Should You Buy?
 After three months of testing eight NAS units across multiple Mac configurations, the Synology DS225+ remains my top recommendation as the best NAS for Time Machine backups in 2026. It nails the SMB3 compatibility, makes Time Machine setup genuinely simple, and runs quietly enough for any home office. For shoppers on tighter budgets, the Synology DS223j delivers the same core Time Machine reliability at a noticeably lower price.
 If you need raw backup speed and large storage capacity for a creative business or media-heavy household, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus with its 10GbE networking and 144TB capacity is the most powerful option here. Whichever model you choose, verify SMB3 support, configure RAID 1 mirroring, and set per-user quotas before your first backup. Your future self will thank you when a drive eventually fails.

NAS for Time Machine: Mac Setup Guide (2026) 
 Skip to content 
 NAS for Time Machine: How to Back Up Your Mac Properly
 Updated: 2026-07-03 
 Time Machine is one of the most forgiving backup tools you can hand a non-technical user, and it stays that way as long as the destination behaves. A single USB drive is fine when there is one Mac in the house, but the moment you have a laptop that wanders off the desk or a second family Mac, a NAS becomes the target that actually keeps up. This guide walks through what that looks like on Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS and Unraid in 2026, and where the usual footguns hide.
 Short version
 Time Machine over NAS talks SMB , the file-sharing protocol Windows has used for decades and macOS now standardises on. Reserve at least twice the size of your Mac's internal SSD, and closer to three or four times if you want more than a couple of months of history. Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS Scale and Unraid all provide native Time Machine targets with per-user quotas, so once the initial share is set up correctly each additional Mac takes about ten minutes.
 SMB, not AFP, and why that matters
 For years, Time Machine over the network used AFP , Apple's own file-sharing protocol, but Apple deprecated AFP as a server-side protocol back in macOS 11 Big Sur and current macOS releases only speak SMB to network backup destinations. In practical terms that means every modern NAS uses SMB3 as the transport, wrapped in a sparse bundle disk image (a growable macOS disk image file that Time Machine expands as your history grows) sitting inside the share.
 The upshot is that if you are shopping for a NAS in 2026, any current model from Synology, QNAP, Asustor, TerraMaster, TrueNAS or Unraid will work, provided its SMB service is set to allow SMB3 and its Bonjour advertising (Apple's automatic service-discovery layer, which is what makes the NAS appear in the Time Machine picker without you typing anything) has the Time Machine flag enabled. Older devices stuck on SMB2 or AFP-only firmware will silently fail with cryptic "Backup volume could not be created" errors; that is nearly always the first thing to check when a fresh setup refuses to connect. Apple's own Time Machine documentation assumes SMB throughout.
 How much storage Time Machine actually needs
 Time Machine does not keep a single snapshot of your Mac; it keeps an incremental history, holding hourly snapshots for a day, daily snapshots for a month, and weekly snapshots for as long as the volume has room. That means the sizing question is really about how deep a history you want, not how big your Mac is. Apple's own guidance, echoed on the Time Machine Wikipedia article , is that the destination should be at least twice the size of the source, and that is the number to start from.
 Minimum, 2x Mac storage: 1 TB Mac maps to a 2 TB quota, enough for a couple of weeks of usable history.
 Recommended, 3-4x: the same 1 TB Mac maps to 3-4 TB, which is where you get roughly a year of meaningful history without Time Machine starting to prune aggressively.
 Heavy users (large video files, frequent Lightroom edits, developer working directories): 5x and up, because a lot of your daily churn is huge files that Time Machine cannot deduplicate efficiently.
 If you have four Macs on one NAS and set no quotas, Time Machine can quietly eat 12-15 TB before you notice, and one laptop can end up occupying most of the share. Setting a per-user quota on the shared folder is not optional in a household with more than one Mac; it is the difference between a backup system that keeps working and one that silently stops making backups.
 Setup on Synology DSM 7
 Synology's DSM has the most polished Time Machine flow of any NAS OS, largely because DSM ships with a "Bonjour Time Machine broadcast" toggle that handles the discovery advertising for you. The full path is Control Panel → File Services → SMB, where you enable the SMB service and then, under Advanced, tick the Bonjour Time Machine option. Create one DSM user per Mac (Control Panel → User), then create a shared folder called TimeMachine , and finally right-click that folder, choose Edit → Advanced, and set the per-user Time Machine folder-size limit to your chosen 2-4x number. Point each Mac at the share via System Settings → Time Machine → Add Backup Disk, and the share will appear once Bonjour has broadcast it.
 Setup on TrueNAS Scale, Unraid and QNAP
 On TrueNAS Scale you create a dataset with the quota you want, create an SMB share on that dataset, and pick the "Multi-protocol shares (AFP/SMB)" or "Time Machine compatible" purpose; TrueNAS then sets the right SMB flags automatically. Because TrueNAS does not always advertise Bonjour by default, you may need to add the share on the Mac by typing smb://truenas.local/timemachine directly into the Time Machine picker rather than waiting for it to appear.
 Unraid handles the same thing through its Community Apps store: install the Time Machine plugin, pick the disk it should back up to, and set a per-user quota inside the plugin's UI. QNAP's QTS is closest in feel to Synology: File Station → create shared folder → tick "Enable this shared folder as Time Machine backup folder", set a size limit, done. All three approaches end up in the same place: an SMB share with a Time Machine flag and a quota.
 Ubiquiti's UNAS line handles this natively as well. UniFi Drive issues separate file-service credentials per user account and exposes a shared drive as a Time Machine target over SMB, which is about as few steps as this gets on any platform. The two-bay UNAS 2 at $199 makes a sensible dedicated backup box if you want Time Machine off your main NAS entirely, and it runs on PoE so it can sit on the switch that is already behind your UPS. Just remember that it does nothing else, so a Mac household that also wanted Plex will still need a second machine.
 Sizing the volume itself
 For a single Mac at home the maths is straightforward. A Mac with a 256 GB SSD is more than covered by a 1 TB Time Machine volume, and a Mac with a 1 TB SSD wants somewhere between 4 and 6 TB of destination so that history has room to grow. A two-bay Synology with two 8 TB drives in a mirror gives 8 TB usable, which is comfortable headroom for two or three Macs in the same household.
 For a family or small studio with four Macs the picture changes. If each Mac gets a 4 TB quota, a four-bay unit populated with 8 TB drives in SHR-1 or RAID 5 gives roughly 24 TB usable after parity, enough to hold all four backups with room for the NAS to serve other things at the same time. This is the size class where RAID 5, SHR-1 or RAID-Z1 stops being overkill and starts being sensible; a single-drive failure would otherwise mean all four Macs lose their backup history at once.
 Common issues and fixes
 The single most common failure is the "Backup volume could not be created" error, and nine times out of ten it is an SMB-version mismatch: macOS refuses to fall back to SMB2 for Time Machine, so if the NAS is defaulting to SMB2 the connection dies before the backup starts. Force the NAS's SMB service to allow SMB3 and the error goes away.
 The second most common is the connection dropping mid-backup, which is almost always Mac-side power management rather than the NAS. Under System Settings → Battery (or Energy Saver on a desktop), enable "Wake for network access" and Power Nap so the Mac keeps the connection alive during scheduled backup windows. If backups appear to slow down over weeks, the usual cause is that the sparse bundle has grown near the quota and Time Machine is spending its cycles pruning old snapshots to make room; the fix is to raise the quota, not to reduce backup frequency. And when the "Backup verifying" state hangs for hours after a restore, that is expected: verification checks every band in the sparse bundle and can genuinely take that long on a large history.
 Performance tips
 Because Time Machine's workload is dominated by tiny metadata operations rather than sequential throughput, an SSD read/write cache in front of the NAS array makes a much bigger difference here than it does for, say, Plex. On the network side, the first backup of a fresh 1 TB Mac takes roughly four hours over gigabit Ethernet and about ninety minutes over 2.5 GbE, so the practical advice is to run that first backup over a wired connection (Ethernet cable or a Thunderbolt-to-Ethernet adapter) and then let WiFi handle the small daily deltas afterwards.
 For the more technical crowd: on TrueNAS Scale, setting the dataset's record size to 1 M and enabling zstd compression on the Time Machine dataset noticeably reduces the on-disk footprint of the sparse bundle without hurting restore performance, because the bundle's band files compress well.
 NAS alone is not enough
 Time Machine on a NAS protects you against a dead Mac, and that is genuinely the most common failure mode, but it does nothing for a dead NAS, a house fire, a burglary, or ransomware that reaches the SMB share. That is the whole point of the 3-2-1 rule (three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy off-site), and it applies here just as much as anywhere else. A cloud service like Backblaze B2 syncing the important user folders off the NAS, or a second NAS at a relative's house pulling nightly snapshots, closes the gap that Time Machine alone cannot. See the backup strategies guide for how to build that second leg.
 Sizing the backup volume Time Machine wants 2–3× your Mac’s disk. Two 8 TB drives, RAID 1 against SHR-1. 
 Open calculator → 
 Recommendation by setup
 One Mac at home: a two-bay Synology DS224+ with 2× 8 TB drives in a mirror lands around six hundred dollars all-in and gives you eight terabytes of usable, redundant Time Machine storage, comfortably enough for a 1 TB laptop with several years of history.
 Two to three Macs in a family: step up to a four-bay Synology DS923+ populated with 4× 8 TB drives in SHR-1, set a per-user quota, and you have about 24 terabytes usable at roughly $1,100, enough to keep all household Macs on the same NAS without any one of them starving the others.
 Small studio or heavy pros: a four-bay TrueNAS or Unraid build with RAID-Z1 across 4× 16 TB drives and a 1 TB SSD cache lands around $1,500 and gives you the room and the metadata performance to back up multiple pros pushing large project files daily.
 Frequently asked questions
 How much storage does Time Machine on NAS need? Minimum 2x Mac storage, recommended 3-4x for usable history. 1 TB Mac -> 3-4 TB Time Machine quota. With multiple Macs always set per-user quota.
 Does Time Machine work over SMB or AFP? SMB. Apple deprecated AFP for Time Machine starting macOS 11. SMB3 is required for current macOS. All modern NAS support it.
 Which NAS are Time Machine compatible? Synology DSM (all models), QNAP QTS, TrueNAS Scale, Unraid with plugin, OMV. SMB3 support and Bonjour broadcast for auto-discovery are key.
 How long does the first Time Machine backup take? With 1 TB Mac data: ~4 hours on 1 GbE, ~1.5 hours on 2.5 GbE. Wired for the first backup, then incremental WiFi is fine.
 Is Time Machine alone enough for backup? No. Time Machine protects against a dead Mac but not NAS failure, fire, or ransomware. 3-2-1 rule: add cloud or a second NAS off-site.

 RAM is the ceiling on Docker, VMs and photo indexing. Two things to check: the shipped amount, and whether it is upgradable. The DS223j and DS223 are fixed at 1 GB forever, while the DXP2800, TS-264 and AS6702T take standard SODIMMs.
 If you see containers in your future, buy upgradable RAM or 8 GB on day one. It is the one spec you cannot fix later on the cheaper models.
 3. Get 2.5GbE if your network can use it
 Gigabit caps you at about 110 MB/s. A 2.5GbE port lifts that to roughly 280 MB/s, and USB 2.5GbE adapters for your computer are inexpensive. Most of the picks above now include it, which tells you where the market is going.
 You need the rest of the chain to match: a 2.5GbE switch and a 2.5GbE port on the computer you copy from. Otherwise the faster port sits idle.
 4. Understand your RAID options
 On a 2-bay you have three sensible choices. RAID 1 mirrors both drives, halving capacity but surviving a drive failure. RAID 0 pools them for full capacity and zero protection, which I never recommend for irreplaceable files. JBOD spans drives with no redundancy.
 Synology adds SHR and QNAP adds TRAID, both of which mix drive sizes more gracefully. On a 2-bay, the practical differences are small; RAID 1 is the right answer for almost every home user.
 Remember that RAID is not backup. It protects against a dead drive, not against deletion, ransomware or a power spike. Keep a second copy of anything you cannot lose, ideally off-site.
 5. Weigh the software ecosystem heavily
 You will interact with the software far more than the hardware. Synology DSM is the most polished and best documented. UGREEN UGOS is friendlier than expected. QNAP QTS is the most powerful and the densest. ASUSTOR ADM sits in the middle, and TerraMaster TOS 6 has improved a lot.
 Read the app list for the jobs you care about before buying. Photo backup quality, surveillance support and Docker tooling vary more between brands than any spec sheet suggests.
 6. Do not ignore noise and power draw
 A home NAS runs 24/7, so both numbers matter. Expect 11 to 18 W idle for most 2-bay units with drives, roughly 10 to 20 dollars a year in electricity. All-flash builds like the AS5402T idle under 10 W.
 Noise is the bigger comfort factor. Fan curves on the ASUSTOR and QNAP units spike more than I would like. If the box will live in a bedroom or living room, check reviews for fan noise, not just benchmarks.
 2-Bay or 4-Bay: which should you actually buy
 This is the single most debated question in home NAS forums, and the honest answer is that a 2-bay is right for most households. Two bays give you RAID 1 protection, a small footprint, lower power draw and a lower entry price. If your library sits under about 8 TB and you want backup plus a media server, a 2-bay covers you for years.
 Go 4-bay if any of these apply: your media library is past 8 TB and growing, you want RAID 5 to keep three-quarters of your raw capacity, you plan to expand drive-by-drive over time, or you intend to run VMs and heavy containers.
 Forum regulars often say they wished they had bought more bays. My counter after testing both: an undersized 4-bay you never fill costs more up front and wastes more power than a well-specced 2-bay you outgrow and then hand down. Buy for the next five years, not the next fifteen.
 The Right Drives Matter as Much as the NAS
 Every NAS above ships diskless, so the drives are half the decision. Two rules cover almost everyone: buy NAS-rated drives, and make sure they are CMR rather than SMR.
 Seagate IronWolf is my default for home use. I have run well over a hundred terabytes of IronWolf drives through various enclosures and the failure rate has been excellent. They include three years of data recovery service, which is real peace of mind for family photos.
 WD Red Plus is the equivalent CMR option and the other safe choice. Avoid the plain WD Red line for RAID, because those are SMR drives and their slow sustained writes can cause RAID rebuilds to fail or time out. For heavier workloads, WD Red Pro and IronWolf Pro add faster spin rates and higher workload ratings.
 For capacity, size your pair to your five-year need, because RAID 1 gives you half the raw total. Two 4 TB drives suit a documents-and-photos household. Two 8 TB drives fit a serious media library, and two 12 TB drives buy you years of headroom.
 Do not forget the third copy of the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy off-site. A NAS plus an external USB drive rotated to a relative’s house covers it cheaply.
 Setting Up Remote Access: Your Private Cloud in 5 Steps
 Remote access is the feature nobody covers properly and everybody wants. It is the difference between a NAS that only works at home and a genuine private cloud. Here is the setup I use, which takes about 15 minutes.
 1. Claim a relay service. Enable QuickConnect on Synology, myQNAPcloud on QNAP, or the equivalent on UGREEN and ASUSTOR. These relay services route your connection without opening anything on your router.
 2. Never port-forward the admin interface. Exposing the admin page directly to the internet is how NAS boxes get hijacked. The relay handles external access safely.
 3. Turn on HTTPS and two-factor authentication. Both are one-click in every OS listed here. Two-factor stops a leaked password from becoming a data breach.
 4. Install the mobile app and enable camera-roll backup. Point it at Wi-Fi only if you have a data cap. Photos then sync automatically in the background whenever you are home.
 5. Add a UPS. A small uninterruptible power supply protects against corruption during a power cut, which is the most common cause of sudden data loss I see. Every brand here supports auto-shutdown when the UPS battery runs low.
 Once it is running, you get file access from anywhere, photo backups from every family phone, and shared links you control. That is the entire value proposition of a home NAS in one sentence.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best 2-bay NAS for home use in 2026?
 The Synology DiskStation DS225+ is the best 2-bay NAS for home use in 2026. Its DSM software makes photo backup, remote access and media streaming genuinely easy, and its 2.5GbE port keeps transfers quick. The UGREEN NASync DXP2800 is the best alternative if you want stronger hardware for the money.
 Is a 2-bay NAS good enough for home use?
 Yes, for most households. A 2-bay NAS with two 8 TB drives in RAID 1 gives you 8 TB of protected storage, which holds roughly 2 million photos. Two bays cover backup, a family media server and private cloud duty for years. Move to a 4-bay only if your library exceeds 8 TB or you want RAID 5 capacity efficiency.
 What is the best NAS setup for home use?
 Start with two identical NAS-rated drives in RAID 1 for mirroring, enable automatic camera-roll backup on every family phone, switch on remote access through the manufacturer relay rather than port forwarding, add two-factor authentication, and connect the NAS to a UPS. Finally, keep one copy of your irreplaceable files off-site to complete the 3-2-1 backup rule.
 What drives should I buy for my 2-bay NAS?
 Buy NAS-rated CMR drives: Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Plus are the two proven choices for home use. Avoid SMR drives like the plain WD Red line in RAID, because their slow sustained writes can cause rebuild failures. Two 4 TB drives suit documents and photos, two 8 TB drives fit a media library, and you only get half the raw capacity in RAID 1.
 Can I use a 2-bay NAS as a Plex server?
 Yes, if the CPU is up to the job. Intel-based models with Quick Sync, such as the UGREEN DXP2800, QNAP TS-264 and TerraMaster F2-425, handle multiple 1080p transcodes and lighter 4K work. ARM-based models like the Synology DS223j and QNAP TS-233 are direct-play only. Configure clients to direct play where possible and any NAS will cope.
 Do I need RAID on a home NAS?
 You do not strictly need it, but RAID 1 is worth using on a 2-bay. It mirrors your data across both drives, so a single drive failure costs you a drive swap rather than your photo library. Just remember RAID is not backup: it will not save you from deletion, ransomware or theft, so keep a separate copy of anything irreplaceable.
 Is a NAS better than paying for cloud storage?
 For a family with more than about 1 TB of data, a NAS usually wins on cost within two to three years compared with monthly cloud subscriptions, and it gives you faster local access plus media streaming. Cloud storage still wins for off-site protection and zero maintenance. The strongest setup is both: a NAS as your main store, with a cloud tier or rotated external drive for the off-site copy.
 What is the Synology drive controversy?
 Synology now restricts official drive compatibility lists on its newer models to Synology-branded drives, which cost more per terabyte than standard Seagate IronWolf or WD Red drives. Third-party drives generally still work, but you lose access to some official support and drive-health integration. The models in this guide work well with standard NAS drives, and I use them myself.
 Final Verdict
 After a year of swapping these ten boxes in and out of my home network, the rankings held steady. The Synology DS225+ is the best 2-bay NAS for home use overall because its software removes every excuse for not backing up your family’s files. The Synology DS223j is the value pick if backup is the whole job, and the UGREEN NASync DXP2800 is the performance pick when you want the most hardware for your money.
 The enthusiast alternatives earned their places too. The QNAP TS-264 for dual 2.5GbE and HDMI, the ASUSTOR AS6702T for expansion headroom, and the TerraMaster F2-425 for buyers who will trade software polish for better components. Beginners should still start with the UGREEN DH2300 or a Synology, because a NAS you can actually set up beats a faster one sitting in a drawer.
 Whichever enclosure you pick, do not cheap out on the drives. Two NAS-rated CMR drives in RAID 1, a UPS on the power bar, and one off-site copy is the setup that has kept my family’s files safe through two drive failures and one power cut. Buy for the next five years, and the box you choose today will still be quietly earning its keep in 2026 and well beyond.

 Mac-Specific Compatibility: Why DSM and Time Machine SMB Matter

Synology’s DSM and QNAP’s QTS both expose SMB shares that macOS recognizes natively, while cheaper firmware like WD My Cloud required workarounds that broke after updates.

 RAID Levels and SHR: How Much Redundancy Do You Actually Need?
 RAID 1 mirrors two drives and survives one failure. RAID 5 stripes across three or more drives and survives one failure while using more capacity. RAID 6 survives two failures. Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR) is a flexible version of RAID 1 that lets you mix drive sizes without wasting space.
 For most Mac households, SHR with two drives or RAID 5 with four drives is the right balance. RAID 0 gives you speed but zero redundancy, so avoid it for backups.
 Drive Count and Capacity: 2-Bay vs 4-Bay for Mac Workflows
 A 2-bay NAS holds up to about 40 TB with modern drives, which covers most households. A 4-bay NAS unlocks RAID 5 or RAID 6 and gives you meaningful room to grow. If you shoot video on a Mac or maintain a multi-Mac household, the 4-bay option pays for itself the first time a drive fails.
 Network Speed: Is 2.5GbE Worth the Upgrade for Backups?
 Gigabit Ethernet caps Time Machine at about 115 MB/s. A 2.5 GbE link raises that ceiling to about 280 MB/s, and a 10 GbE link pushes it past 1 GB/s. For Mac users with SSDs and large backups, faster networking cuts overnight backup windows dramatically.

 Software Ecosystem: What DSM 7 and UGOS Pro Actually Deliver
 Synology’s DSM 7 remains the most polished macOS-friendly NAS operating system. It handles Time Machine, Mac file sharing via AFP and SMB, iPhone photos via Synology Photos, and bare-metal restores via Active Backup. UGOS Pro covers the same bases but with rougher edges and a faster release cadence.
 For non-technical Mac users, DSM 7 is the safer pick. For tinkerers who want stronger hardware at a lower price, UGOS Pro delivers more raw value.

 Which NAS works best with Mac?
 Synology’s DiskStation models with DSM 7 are the most reliable NAS for Mac in 2026. Time Machine works plug-and-play over SMB, and the macOS integration is the deepest in the category. For a single-Mac household, the DS225+ is our top pick.
 What is the best backup system for a Mac?
 A NAS with native Time Machine support beats external drives and cloud subscriptions for most Mac users. It gives you automatic, redundant backups without monthly fees, faster restore times than iCloud, and remote access from anywhere.
 Which NAS is best for backups?
 The Synology DS225+ is the best overall NAS for backups in 2026, combining an Intel CPU, fast transfers, and excellent DSM 7 software. Budget buyers should consider the Synology DS223j. Power users with multi-Mac households should consider the DS425+ or UGREEN DXP4800 Plus.
 How do I set up Time Machine on a NAS?
 Open DSM or your NAS OS, create a dedicated Time Machine user, enable SMB on the shared folder, then on your Mac open Time Machine settings, click Add Backup Disk, and pick the NAS share. The first backup can take several hours.
 Do all NAS work with Mac Time Machine?
 No. Some cheaper NAS units fail to expose proper SMB shares or handle APFS sparse bundles correctly. Stick with Synology, QNAP, or UGREEN for reliable Time Machine support. WD My Cloud and similar units have a track record of inconsistent Mac behavior.
 Final Verdict: Which NAS Should You Buy for Your Mac?
 If you run a single Mac and want a set-and-forget Time Machine destination, the Synology DS225+ is the best balance of price, performance, and software polish. Budget-conscious buyers will get the same Time Machine experience from the Synology DS223j at a lower price. Power users with multiple Macs and large media libraries should consider the Synology DS425+ or UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus for 4-bay scalability and faster networking.

Home Backup NAS Buying Guide (2026) — ChooseCompute Skip to content All guides Best NAS for Home Use, Backup & Mac/PC (2026 Buying Guide)
 Compare home backup NAS builds for Mac and Windows: complete hardware costs, protected capacity, backup software limits, and a tested second copy.
 Research updated 2026-09-07
 A home NAS should be easy to maintain, large enough for several years of growth, and paired with a second backup destination. Whether backing up Windows PCs, Mac Time Machine, or family mobile devices, RAID reduces downtime after a drive failure but does not replace an independent backup.
 Research-backed builds by tier
 Each article combines the exact NAS and HDD records with official facts, independent reviews, YouTube material, and community discussion.

 About 24 TB usable · $1,734.96 reference total

 Read the full tier analysis → High-end DS1825+ + 6 × 16 TB
 About 64 TB usable · $5,503.99 reference total

 Read the full tier analysis → 
 Questions to answer first
 1 How much data exists across every home PC, Mac, phone, and external drive? 
 2 How many years of file history and snapshots should remain available? 
 3 Where will the independent second copy live? 
 How to choose
 Start with current data, add three to five years of growth, then keep roughly 20% free.
 Choose two bays for a simple mirror; choose four bays when capacity will grow or multiple jobs share the NAS.
 Prefer straightforward backup software and administration over unused processor features.
 Avoid these mistakes
 Treating RAID as the only backup
 Buying raw capacity instead of protected capacity
 Ignoring restore testing
 Frequently asked questions
 Is a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 a complete backup solution?
 No. A mirror keeps a copy on each disk so the NAS can usually continue after one disk fails. Deletion, malware, theft, and enclosure failure can affect both copies. Keep versioned backups on a separate USB disk, another NAS, or a cloud destination, with at least one copy off-site. Test that you can restore a file before relying on the setup.
 What is the best NAS for backing up multiple Mac (Time Machine) and Windows PCs?
 Our entry DS223 build fits ordinary file backup and Mac Time Machine when a 4TB mirror is enough. Choose the DS925+ when you need more capacity, spare bays, or supported business backup packages. Check each Windows backup application against the exact NAS model: Synology Drive file sync is different from a full computer image, and Active Backup for Business is not available on every DiskStation.
 How much usable storage do I actually get from 2×4TB or 4×12TB drives?
 Two 4TB disks in RAID 1 provide 4TB decimal capacity, equivalent to about 3.64TiB before system and filesystem overhead. Four 12TB disks in RAID 5 provide 36TB, about 32.74TiB before overhead. TB and TiB are different units; that conversion is not space lost to formatting. Leave room for backup versions, snapshots, and future growth.
 Synology vs. UGREEN for beginner home backup: Which is easier?
 Choose Synology when its integrated backup applications match your computers and you value a familiar administration workflow. UGREEN can offer more CPU and networking for the budget, but check application support and the recovery process before choosing on specifications alone. Both need updates, alerts, and restore tests; neither is maintenance-free.
 How do I protect my NAS backup against ransomware and sudden power outages?
 Use separate administrator and backup accounts, versioned backups, and an off-site or offline copy. Snapshots help recover older versions; immutable retention is a separate feature that must be supported by the exact model and configured correctly. A compatible UPS with tested automatic shutdown can reduce interruption risk. Neither snapshots nor a UPS guarantees recovery on its own.

Best replacements for Time Capsule backup 2027 
 Mac owners upgrading to macOS 27 will need to replace their AirPort Time Capsule for Time Machine backups. We picked five diskless NAS enclosures that cost less than $300 to fit the bill. 
 Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14 without support for Apple Filing Protocol, or AFP. AirPort Time Capsule and AirPort Disk depend on AFP for Time Machine backups. 
 The company's updated support document says Time Machine continues to work with third-party network-attached storage devices that support Server Message Block, or SMB. The five options below support network backups from a Mac, although availability and sale prices can change. 
 These prices cover the enclosures rather than complete storage systems. Buyers must add at least one compatible drive and connect the NAS to an existing router through Ethernet. 
 The macOS change doesn't disable the AirPort's router or Wi-Fi hardware. It specifically prevents Macs running macOS 27 from using an AirPort Time Capsule or AirPort Disk as a Time Machine destination. 
 Some of these will work as routers, properly configured. We leave this, and a debate about the security of doing this, as an exercise for the reader 
 They also don't provide Wi-Fi, like a Time Capsile does. The Time Capsule is so far out of support at this point, though, you've probably already moved on from that. 
 Anyone with files stored only in an existing Time Capsule backup should restore them before upgrading. Keep the old backup intact until the replacement NAS has completed a full backup and successfully restored a test file. 
 Here's what we've done. We took the original retail price of the fifth generation Time Capsule, adjusted to 2026 dollars, and subtracted a bit more than $100 for the drive of your choice, and rounded down to $300. 
 All of these network attached storage devices come in under that cost. 
 TerraMaster F2-425 offers the most processing headroom
 The TerraMaster F2-425 provides two SATA drive bays, an Intel N5095 quad-core processor, 4GB of DDR4 memory, and 2.5GbE networking. 
 TerraMaster allows owners to expand the memory to 16GB, giving the F2-425 room for services beyond file storage. It supports Docker, hardware-assisted 4K video transcoding, and TerraMaster's TRAID storage system. 
 TOS 7 includes a Time Machine Backup tool that turns an authorized folder into a network backup destination. Time Machine Backup is disabled by default and must be enabled during setup. 
 TerraMaster F2-425 2-Bay NAS review: It uses two bays with tool-free sleds 
 Our review gave the F2-425 four out of five stars for its performance, memory expansion, and virtualization support. Its two-drive limit restricts the available RAID configurations, but RAID 1 can protect a Time Machine volume against the failure of one drive. 
 Buy TerraMaster F2-425 
 The F2-425 is the strongest option for someone who needs network backups now and may later add a media server, Home Assistant, or other self-hosted software. 
 The TerraMaster F2-425 is available from B&H Photo and Amazon.com for $254.99 at press time, down from $299.99. 
 Ugreen NASync DH2300 is the easiest starting point
 The Ugreen DH2300 targets people buying their first NAS. Its iPhone-assisted setup removes much of the address hunting and browser configuration that can make network storage intimidating. 
 An eight-core Rockchip RK3576 processor and 4GB of fixed memory run UGOS Pro. Connectivity includes Gigabit Ethernet, USB-C, two USB-A ports, and an HDMI output capable of driving a 4K display. 
 Ugreen NASync DH2300 top-down view of the two drive bays 
 UGOS Pro supports Time Machine backups from a Mac over SMB. Ugreen also includes phone backups, remote file access, media applications, and local photo organization. 
 Buy Ugreen NASync DH2300 
 The DH2300 doesn't support Docker or memory upgrades, so it isn't intended to become a demanding home server. Our review awarded it four out of five stars and found that its hardware was fast enough for secure file serving and ordinary household backups. 
 The DH2300 is the most approachable choice for someone who wants automatic Mac backups without extensive NAS administration. 
 The Ugreen NASync DH2300 is available from Ugreen direct for $227.99 and from Amazon.com , where pricing can vary. 
 LincStation E1 combines SATA and NVMe storage
 The LincStation E1 combines two SATA drive bays and two M.2 NVMe slots. LincPlus calls it a four-bay NAS, although only two bays accept conventional hard drives. 
 The combination supports inexpensive hard drives alongside faster solid-state storage. A Rockchip RK3568 quad-core processor and 4GB of fixed memory run LincOS. 
 The enclosure also provides 2.5GbE, HDMI, Wi-Fi 5, and three USB-A connections. 
 LincPlus LincStation E1 rear USB-A, HDMI, and Ethernet ports 
 Time Machine worked with the unit we tested, but LincPlus doesn't document the feature as clearly as TerraMaster, Ugreen, Synology, or Qnap. Buyers should confirm that current LincOS firmware still exposes an SMB-compatible Time Machine destination. 
 Buy LincStation E1 
 LincPlus doesn't offer a macOS management client. Mac owners must administer the NAS through its local web interface, while the company's iPhone, iPad, Android, or Windows software handles built-in remote access. 
 The unusual mix of SATA and NVMe storage gives the E1 more flexibility than a conventional two-bay NAS. Its limited processor and developing software make it a better fit for basic storage than demanding server applications. 
 The LincStation E1 is listed through the LincPlus store for $169, down from $219. An Amazon listing is also available, with price and stock subject to change. 
 Synology DiskStation DS223j emphasizes mature software
 The Synology DS223j is a two-bay diskless enclosure. Its 1GB of fixed memory and Gigabit Ethernet limit heavier workloads, but Synology's established DiskStation Manager software remains its main advantage. 
 The DS223j uses a 1.7GHz Realtek RTD1619B quad-core processor. Both bays accept 3.5-inch SATA hard drives, while 2.5-inch drives require optional holders. 
 Synology also supports Btrfs and snapshots on the DS223j 
 DiskStation Manager supports Time Machine through SMB and lets an administrator place storage quotas on individual backup users. Quotas prevent one Mac's backup history from consuming the entire shared volume. 
 Buy Synology DiskStation DS223j 
 Synology also supports Btrfs and snapshots on the DS223j. File self-healing requires a storage pool with redundant data, such as mirrored drives, rather than Btrfs alone. 
 The DS223j is the conservative choice for users who value documentation, software maturity, and a large application ecosystem more than faster networking. 
 The Synology DiskStation DS223j is available from B&H Photo for $209.99 and from Amazon.com , where pricing can vary. 
 QNAP TS-216G puts 2.5GbE near the price limit
 The Qnap TS-216G combines two SATA drive bays with a 2.5GbE port. It uses a 2GHz Arm Cortex-A55 quad-core processor and 4GB of memory. 
 Qnap recorded SMB transfers of up to 291MB per second in laboratory testing with SATA SSDs, RAID 1, 2.5GbE, and a Windows Server client. A Mac connected through ordinary Gigabit Ethernet won't reach those speeds. 
 The TS-216G officially supports Time Machine, and Qnap provides instructions for creating a dedicated backup user and shared folder through QTS. Its setup guide directs users to enable SMB 3 before selecting the shared folder in Time Machine. 
 Buy QNAP TS-216G 
 Qnap also includes snapshots, mobile photo backups, USB one-touch copying, and an NPU for recognizing faces and objects in stored photos. Its hot-swappable bays allow a failed drive to be replaced without shutting down the NAS when the storage configuration can tolerate the failure. 
 The TS-216G is the best fit for a household with several Macs or an existing 2.5GbE network. Its extensive settings and applications provide flexibility, but they also create a steeper learning curve. 
 Qnap recorded SMB transfers of up to 291MB per second 
 The Qnap TS-216G is available from B&H Photo and Amazon.com for $299. 
 A drive connected to your router isn't a universal replacement
 Some consumer routers can share an attached USB drive as a Time Machine destination, but support and safety depends on the exact model. Check the router's manual for explicit Time Machine over SMB support before relying on it for macOS 27 backups. 
 Owners who bought and configured their own routers may have compatible hardware. Most ISP-provided gateways don't offer the required storage and backup controls, so customers using one probably won't have much luck there. 
 Drives and RAID increase the final cost
 All five NAS devices above are sold without user storage. Adding one drive provides the lowest initial cost, while two matching drives allow RAID 1 to preserve access if one drive fails. 
 RAID 1 writes the same data to both drives, but it doesn't protect against deletion, theft, fire, malware, or failure of the NAS itself. Irreplaceable files still need another local or off-site copy. 
 The AirPort Time Capsule combined a router and a hard drive, making a Time Machine destination in one device. We're still testing the third-party patch that adds SMB3 to the older units, making them compatible again. 
 Ultimately, they are just too old to keep relying on. 
 These replacements require more setup, but they are much newer, provide replaceable drives, larger potential capacities, modern SMB support, and more control over Mac backups.
